article.title: The Economics of Reliability: Designing Systems for Failure

paragraphs.en: Perfect reliability is rarely a realistic engineering objective. Redundancy, monitoring, testing, and recovery procedures all have costs, while outages impose costs on customers and organizations. A rational reliability strategy compares the marginal cost of prevention with the expected impact of failure. The comparison is not simple because rare events can have severe consequences, and the cost of reputational damage may be difficult to estimate. Systems should therefore be designed to fail safely and recover predictably.
paragraphs.zh: 本段討論「The Economics of Reliability: Designing Systems for Failure」的實務含義：先理解問題與決策背景。 重要的是將觀察到的現象與真正需要採取的行動分開，並留下可供驗證的依據。
paragraphs.ja: 「The Economics of Reliability: Designing Systems for Failure」について、業務上の前提と意思決定を確認する。まず課題と背景を理解する。 観察事実と実際に取るべき行動を区別し、検証可能な根拠を残すことが重要である。

paragraphs.en: Reliability engineering begins by identifying the services that matter most, the ways they can fail, and the consequences of each failure. A short outage in a noncritical internal dashboard is different from an incorrect payment or a lost customer record. The latter may demand stronger controls even if it occurs rarely. Severity, detectability, and reversibility are therefore as important as the raw frequency of incidents.
